paras: The lynching of Doyral Bryant was the reported hanging of a Black horse trader from Fayetteville, North Carolina, whose body was said to have been found on a tree between Fayetteville and Clinton in January 1881. Papers described the killers only as "parties unknown" and linked the hanging to a murder of which Bryant had been acquitted seven years earlier. A Fayetteville correspondent wrote that the report had been both denied and repeated, and that only Bryant's disappearance was certain.

According to a Fayetteville letter of January 21, a young white man named Charley Boone was found beaten to death on October 15, 1873, in the cabin of Rich Mims on the southern edge of the town. Bryant and Wiley Evans, both described as "mulattos," had spent the evening drinking there with Boone, Mims and a white woman, Fanny Briggs. The two men were tried separately at the following January term of the Cumberland County Superior Court, where Evans confessed to striking Boone with a chair and Bryant was acquitted. The correspondent wrote that public opinion never accepted the verdict and that Bryant, who later lived by horse trading in Fayetteville, "was a marked man."

Some weeks before the letter was written, Bryant set out for a county fair at Clinton, in Sampson County, and was said to have been seen on the road with a crowd of drunken men. He never reached Clinton or returned home. A newspaper in a neighboring county and local talk then reported that his body had been found hanging by a halter from a tree between Fayetteville and Clinton, with two worn-out horses tied nearby and a placard on his back reading "This is the murderer of Charley Moore" [Boone]. The Lumberton Robesonian put it more plainly, saying that Bryant was "found suspended from a limb" there "one day last week."

According to the Fayetteville letter, Bryant's friends had not recovered his body and did not know where he was, and the writer could not say whether the matter would ever be cleared up. No report of an inquest, arrests or a later confirmation was found.

The earliest report found was a one-sentence item in the Wheeling Register on January 24, stating that Bryant "was lynched by parties unknown" and "had once escaped conviction for murder." The long Fayetteville letter ran in the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer on January 25 and in the Chicago Tribune on January 26 under the headline "The Murderer's Reward," which said "retributive justice has at last overtaken him" while doubting that the death was confirmed. In North Carolina, the Raleigh Farmer and Mechanic headed the Robesonian brief "LYNCHED" on January 27, and the Winston-Salem Western Sentinel called it "a real tragedy" the same day. Both North Carolina reprints called Bryant "the man who murdered" the earlier victim without mentioning his acquittal.

The wire item and the Robesonian brief reported the hanging as fact, but the Fayetteville correspondent, writing from Bryant's home town, said the report "has been denied and reiterated over and over" and that only his disappearance was certain. The papers also spelled the names differently, giving the victim as Doyral, Boyral or Doyle Bryant and the man killed in 1873 as Boone, Boole or Moore.

reader.title: Lynching of Doyral Bryant
bases: Papers reported that Bryant was found hanged from a tree, called it a lynching by 'parties unknown', and tied it to a murder of which he had been acquitted (A1, A3, A4).

The wire and the Lumberton Robesonian report Bryant hanged by unknown parties, and the reported placard ('This is the murderer of Charley Moore [Boone]') gives a pretext of punishing an old killing (A1, A3, A4); but the Fayetteville letter says the report had been 'denied and reiterated' and the body was not recovered, and no paper gives the number of killers (A3).

The Robesonian brief and the wire paragraph state the hanging as fact (A1, A4, A5), while the Fayetteville letter says the report had been denied as well as repeated and that only Bryant's disappearance was certain (A3).
